name: Abu Dhabi
summary: Operating as the Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM), this jurisdiction uses the direct application of English common law and provides a flexible, risk-based captive framework. It offers a dedicated rulebook and a streamlined application process with four distinct classes of captive insurers to meet varied business needs. A major benefit is the 0% tax environment guaranteed until 2065, along with the ability to outsource all management functions to ADGM-authorized managers.
tax_notes: 0% tax until 2065; 5% VAT may apply

name: Alabama
summary: Alabama positions itself at the forefront of the industry by offering innovative features like a 60-day provisional license and the ability to form as any entity allowed under law, including Series LLCs. Legislation enacted in 2006 was significantly updated in 2016 to modernize the Alabama Captive Act and enhance competitiveness. The state is active in advocacy through the Alabama Captive Insurance Association and offers prorated premium taxes in the first year.
tax_notes: $100,000 maximum cap; no tax on dormant captives

name: Alberta
summary: Alberta enacted dedicated captive insurance legislation under the Captive Insurance Companies Act (SA 2021, c. C-2.4), which came into force on July 1, 2022, making it the second Canadian province with a standalone captive statute. Administered by the Alberta Superintendent of Insurance (Treasury Board and Finance), the regime authorizes pure, association, and sophisticated insured captives—formed as either corporations or limited partnerships—as well as redomestication of foreign captives. Driven by strong demand from the energy, natural resource, and commercial sectors, along with Canada's lowest provincial corporate income tax rate (8%) and streamlined 6-week licensing, Alberta has rapidly expanded its captive insurance sector. The Superintendent's Captive Insurance Company Licensing Guide, updated November 7, 2025, states that captives may underwrite all classes of insurance except automobile insurance for basic coverage and surety insurance. Canadian Underwriter reported on October 30, 2026 that Hub International senior vice-president Angela Iannetta said Alberta's rules now allow a captive to insure a surety program.
legislation: Captive Insurance Companies Act, SA 2021, c. C-2.4 (in force July 1, 2022) & Captive Insurance Companies Regulation, Alta. Reg. 100/2022
applicable_legislation: Captive Insurance Companies Act (SA 2021, c. C-2.4); Captive Insurance Companies Regulation (Alta. Reg. 100/2022); Captive Insurance Companies (Prescribed Enactments) Regulation (Alta. Reg. 103/2022); Fees Under the Captive Insurance Companies Act Order (Ministerial Order 14/2022); Classes of Insurance Regulation (Alta. Reg. 144/2011); Recovery of Insurance Administration Costs Regulation (Alta. Reg. 102/2022); Insurance Enforcement and Administration Regulation (Alta. Reg. 101/2022); Business Corporations Act (RSA 2000, c. B-9); Partnership Act (RSA 2000, c. P-3); Alberta Corporate Tax Act (RSA 2000, c. A-15).

min_capital.Association Captive: CAD 500,000 minimum base capital (or greater of formulaic revenue/claims thresholds or actuary-proposed risk-based amount; subject to Superintendent's determination)
min_capital.Sophisticated Insured Captive: CAD 500,000 minimum base capital (insureds must demonstrate insurance expertise and pay at least CAD 500,000 in aggregate annual premiums; subject to Superintendent's determination)

tax_notes: Subject to federal and provincial corporate income tax (8% Alberta general corporate tax rate) and Alberta insurance premiums tax under the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (3% on life, accident and sickness insurance; 4% on property, casualty and other insurance contracts on Alberta risks).

name: Anguilla
summary: Anguilla's Insurance Act provides a comprehensive framework for domestic, offshore, and captive insurance, notably including a specific 2018 provision for producer-affiliated reinsurance companies. The domicile offers five sub-categories of Class B licenses, ranging from unrestricted foreign business to single-owner captives. Unless maintaining a permanent local staff, insurers are required to appoint a licensed insurance manager.
tax_notes: Tax-neutral structures for Class B insurers

name: Arizona
summary: Arizona's Captive Insurance Division, in the Department of Insurance and Financial Institutions, licenses captives under Arizona Revised Statutes sections 20-1098 through 20-1098.24. The division states that the captive statute took effect in 2002. A captive may be pure, group, agency, or protected cell, and may be formed as a stock insurer, limited liability company, mutual, reciprocal, or nonprofit. A group captive is an association captive, an industry group captive, or a risk retention group. The statute also provides for branch captives and for dormant captives. Minimum unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus is $250,000 for a pure or protected cell captive and $500,000 for a group, agency, or reciprocal captive. A pure or group captive that transacts only reinsurance holds half of the applicable amount. A dormant captive with a certificate of dormancy holds $125,000. Fees under section 20-167(F) are in lieu of premium tax and other state and local taxes, except taxes on real and tangible personal property located in Arizona, transaction privilege and use taxes, and the section 20-224 premium tax that an agency captive owes on specified life and disability policies to the extent it exceeds those fees. As of 30 June 2026 the division counted 209 captives: 181 pure including reinsurers, 6 protected cell, 5 industry group, 1 association, 4 agency, 12 risk retention groups, and no branch captives. Its growth table lists 14 licenses issued in 2026 beside that cumulative count of 209. The director must approve or deny an application within 30 days after deeming it complete. The governing body meets at least once a year in Arizona, and the captive keeps its principal place of business, books and records, and an Arizona manager in the state.
legislation: Arizona Revised Statutes sections 20-1098 through 20-1098.24 (captive insurers)
applicable_legislation: Arizona Revised Statutes sections 20-1098 through 20-1098.24. Definitions are section 20-1098. Licensing, permitted business, the in-state meeting and principal-place requirements, and the 30-day decision are section 20-1098.01. Minimum capital and surplus are section 20-1098.03. Protected cells are section 20-1098.05. The annual report and audit are section 20-1098.07. The fee-in-lieu and premium-tax rule is section 20-1098.17. Dormancy is section 20-1098.24. Certificate of authority fees for captive insurers are set by the director under section 20-167(F). The Captive Insurance Division states that the captive statute's effective date is 2002. A session-law citation for the original enactment was not retrieved, so 2002 is the effective year the division publishes and is not recorded here as a separately verified enactment year.

min_capital.Pure: At least $250,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus in combination (A.R.S. section 20-1098.03(A)(1)). The division publishes the same floor.
min_capital.Group: At least $500,000 (section 20-1098.03(A)(2)). A group captive insurer is an association captive, an industry group captive, or a risk retention group (section 20-1098(16)). The division lists association and industry group captives, and risk retention groups, at $500,000.
min_capital.Protected cell: At least $250,000 (section 20-1098.03(A)(4)). The division publishes the same floor.
min_capital.Reciprocal: At least $500,000 for a captive insurer organized as a reciprocal insurer (section 20-1098.03(A)(5)).
min_capital.Pure or group, reinsurance only: One-half of the applicable pure or group amount (section 20-1098.03(A)(6)). The division states that pure reinsurers hold 50 percent of the indicated amounts.
min_capital.Dormant: A dormant captive insurer that has been issued a certificate of dormancy maintains unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus of at least $125,000 (section 20-1098.24(B)(1)). A risk retention group is excluded from the dormant-captive definition.
min_capital.Branch: The division lists branch captive insurers as a type and counted none at 30 June 2026. Section 20-1098.03 does not state a separate dollar floor for a branch captive.
min_capital.Form and additional capital: The statutory minimum is cash or an irrevocable and unconditional letter of credit with an evergreen clause, payable to, filed with, and held by the director (section 20-1098.03(B)). The director may prescribe additional capital and surplus based on the type, volume, and nature of insurance (section 20-1098.03(C)).

tax_notes: A.R.S. section 20-1098.17 provides that the captive fees paid under section 20-167(F) are payment in full and in lieu of all other state, county, district, municipal, and school taxes, licenses, and excises, except a tax on real and tangible personal property located in Arizona, the transaction privilege tax and use tax under title 42, chapter 5, articles 1 and 4, and transaction privilege and use taxes imposed by a county, city, or town. An agency captive insurer that insures the life or disability risks specified in section 20-1098.01(A)(3)(b) pays the premium tax prescribed in section 20-224 on those policies to the extent it exceeds the fees paid under section 20-167. The Captive Insurance Division states that Arizona has no insurance premium tax. The annual regulatory charge published by the division is the flat license renewal fee, not a premium-tax rate.
contact_name: Victoria E. Fimea, J.D., Chief Captive Analyst
types_allowed: Pure captive insurers, including pure reinsurers
Captive insurers organized as reciprocal insurers
Dormant captive insurers holding a certificate of dormancy, other than risk retention groups

fees.licensing_incorporation: DIFI's captive payment page lists an original insurer license application total of $1,175 and an original per-cell application of $1,000. The division's fee table lists a $100 examiners' revolving-fund deposit, a $75 charter-document filing fee, and a $60 articles of incorporation or organization fee payable to the Arizona Corporation Commission. The payment page also lists a $200 license-amendment fee and a $30 amended-charter fee. Fees are nonrefundable. The applicant may also be billed for outside specialists used in the review. Section 20-1098.01(J) requires the nonrefundable issuance fee prescribed under section 20-167.
fees.annual_fees: Captive insurer annual license renewal of $5,500, and a protected-cell annual renewal of $2,500, as published by the division and on its payment page. The renewal fee is paid not earlier than 1 July and not later than 1 September (section 20-1098.01(J)). A certificate of dormancy is renewed every five years; the statute points that fee to section 20-167 and the division page does not publish a separate dormancy amount.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No generally applicable captive premium tax. Fees under section 20-167(F) are in lieu of other state and local taxes, subject to the property-tax, transaction-privilege-tax, use-tax, and agency-captive exceptions in section 20-1098.17. The standing annual regulatory charge is the $5,500 license renewal, plus $2,500 for each protected cell.

annual_filing_requirements: Not later than 90 days after the end of its fiscal year, a captive insurer submits a report of its financial condition verified by the oath of two executive officers. The report may use generally accepted accounting principles unless the director requires statutory accounting principles, with any modifications the director requires (A.R.S. section 20-1098.07(A)). Financial statements are audited by an independent certified public accountant unless the director determines that an audit is not necessary, and the audit opinion is filed not later than six months after fiscal year-end. Unless the director grants an exemption, the annual report meets the applicable life and health, property and casualty, or NAIC health actuarial requirements. A protected cell captive also files an accounting of each protected cell with the annual report. A branch captive files, within 60 days after its fiscal year-end, the reports required by its home jurisdiction. A dormant captive with a certificate of dormancy files a verified financial-condition report within 90 days after fiscal year-end. The license renewal fee is due between 1 July and 1 September. The division states that an exemption from the annual actuarial certification and audit may apply to small captive insurers, and that there is no routine statutory examination for pure captive insurers.

name: Arkansas
summary: Arkansas aggressively recruits captives by refining its laws, including major changes in 2017 and 2019 that reduced capital requirements and welcomed RRGs. It is recognized as one of the most cost-effective domiciles, featuring low application and license fees and a $100,000 tax liability cap. The Arkansas Insurance Department offers no-cost preliminary analyses for companies considering captive formation.
tax_notes: $100,000 maximum annual tax liability

name: Aruba
summary: Aruba offers a safe and stable environment for financial services with an international legal framework overseen by the Central Bank of Aruba. Captives are defined as businesses insuring risks originating almost exclusively from shareholders, affiliates, or joint venture participants. Operations must maintain an office in Aruba for financial administration and have at least one managing director residing on the island.

min_capital.General: Subject to Central Bank review and actuarial report

tax_notes: Requires annual audited financial statements

name: Bahrain
summary: Bahrain serves as a regional base for international insurers, with a sector regulated by the Central Bank of Bahrain (CBB) as a single regulator since 2002. The CBB differentiates between captive and commercial insurers, offering lower capital and solvency requirements for captives provided they do not include third-party liability risks. The domicile is supported by a large pool of brokers, actuaries, and insurance managers.

min_capital.Captive: Risk-based; lower than traditional insurers unless third-party liability is involved

tax_notes: Competitive regulatory environment

name: Barbados
summary: Barbados licenses insurers under the Insurance Act, Cap. 310. The Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52 commenced on 1 January 2019, created three licence classes, and repealed the Exempt Insurance Act, Cap. 308A. A Class 1 licensee is an insurance company that underwrites related-party business. A Class 2 licensee includes an insurance company that underwrites third-party risks, and Class 3 covers insurance intermediaries, managers, and holding companies. The Financial Services Commission supervises the sector under the Financial Services Commission Act, 2010-21. The Commission's homepage reported 176 Class 1 licensees at 31 December 2025, compared with 175 at 31 December 2024. It reported 121 Class 2 licensees at 31 December 2025, of which 21 had direct exposure to the Barbadian public, and 815 Class 3 licensees. Class 1 is the related-party population. The Commission does not publish a pure-versus-group split, a cell count, or 2025 figures for new and surrendered Class 1 licences.
legislation: Insurance Act, Cap. 310, as amended by the Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52 (commenced 1 January 2019)
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act, Cap. 310; Insurance (Amendment) Act, 2018-52, which commenced on 1 January 2019 and repealed the Exempt Insurance Act, Cap. 308A; Financial Services Commission Act, 2010-21. Minimum capital and solvency for Class 1 and Class 2 insurers are set out in the Commission's capital and solvency appendix.

An equivalent sum in another currency is allowed if the Commission approves it. Capital must be fully paid up in cash.
min_capital.Class 1 or Class 2, risks and premiums i: BDS $3,000,000 long-term; BDS $3,000,000 general; BDS $5,000,000 long-term and general; BDS $1,000,000 motor vehicle only; BDS $1,000,000 industrial life.
min_capital.Segregated cell company, Barbados reinsu: A Class 1 or Class 2 segregated cell company licensed to carry on reinsurance of risks located in Barbados, with premiums originating in Barbados, must have aggregate paid-up capital of BDS $3,000,000, and each cell must have minimum paid-up capital of BDS $500,000.
min_capital.Solvency, risks and premiums outside Bar: In the first financial year, assets must exceed liabilities by BDS $250,000. After that year, assets must exceed liabilities by BDS $250,000 if the preceding year's premium income did not exceed BDS $1,500,000; by one-fifth of that premium income if it exceeded BDS $1,500,000 but did not exceed BDS $10,000,000; or by BDS $2,000,000 plus one-tenth of the amount by which premium income exceeded BDS $10,000,000.

tax_notes: The Barbados Revenue Authority publishes corporate income tax at 0 percent for Class 1 insurance companies, 2 percent for Class 2 insurance companies, and 2 percent for Class 3 insurance companies. The same table still shows 0 percent for exempt insurance companies and 0.35 percent for qualifying insurance companies that were licensed under the Insurance Act, Cap. 310 and carrying on life insurance business before 17 October 2017. No separate captive premium tax was stated on the Revenue Authority corporations page or the Commission pages used.

name: Bermuda
summary: Bermuda's captive classes are supervised by the Bermuda Monetary Authority under the Insurance Act 1978. Class 1 is a single-parent general captive writing only the risks of its owners and their affiliates. Class 2 covers multi-owner captives and captives writing no more than 20 percent of net premiums from unrelated risks. Class 3 covers captives writing more than 20 percent, and up to 49 percent, of net premiums from unrelated risks, together with certain third-party writers that are not commercial Class 3A, 3B, or 4 insurers. Class A and Class B are the long-term equivalents of Class 1 and Class 2. The Authority's 2025 annual report gives 2025 register counts of 159 Class 1, 244 Class 2, 180 Class 3, 12 Class A, and 13 Class B insurers, 608 in those captive classes. The 2024 column of the same table is 632 and matches the report's market statistics for the year ended 31 December 2024. Single-parent captives are the Class 1 and Class A counts, 171 in the 2025 column, which is the same pairing the report used for its 31 December 2024 company-type table. Class 3, 180, is the third-party captive category. Class 2 and Class B together are 257 and mix multi-owner captives with captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated premiums, so that pair is not stored as a group-captive count. New captive-class registrations in the 2025 column were 2 Class 1, 5 Class 2, 1 Class 3, 1 Class A, and no Class B, 9 in total. The report does not publish surrenders. Its 2023 captive insight report, published in December 2025, said segregated and incorporated segregated accounts were in excess of 2,000 and that 15 percent of captive-market companies operated as segregated accounts or incorporated segregated accounts companies. That report does not give an exact cell count, and the 2025 annual report does not update it.
legislation: Insurance Act 1978, and the Insurance Returns and Solvency Regulations 1980
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act 1978, including section 17 on statutory financial statements and section 18 on statutory financial returns; Insurance Returns and Solvency Regulations 1980, Schedule I (general-business solvency margin) and Schedule II (long-term minimum margin of solvency); Bermuda Monetary Authority Act 1969, Fourth Schedule, for fees effective 1 January 2026; Corporate Income Tax Act 2023; Bermuda Monetary Authority Guidance Note, General Business Insurers with Segregated Accounts and Separate Accounts (September 2026), issued under section 2B of the Insurance Act 1978, for financial years commencing on or after 1 January 2027. It applies to limited-purpose and commercial insurers in the general-business licence classes that maintain segregated accounts under the Segregated Accounts Companies Act 2000 or separate accounts permitted for insurers incorporated under a private act. It does not apply to long-term insurers. Incorporated segregated account companies and incorporated segregated account insurers remain under the separate guidance note issued in December 2020. Where this note and the Special Purpose Insurer guidance note issued on 1 July 2020 do not align, the Special Purpose Insurer note takes precedence for that class. The Authority will consider transitional applications in the first year after implementation. Bermuda Monetary Authority Notice, Agreed Upon Procedures for Segregated Account and Separate Account General Business Insurers (23 September 2026).

min_capital.Class 1: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, the greater of a premium-based formula and a reserve-based formula, subject to a $120,000 floor.
min_capital.Class 2: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, subject to a $250,000 floor.
min_capital.Class 3: Minimum capital and surplus at least equal to the minimum solvency margin, subject to a $1,000,000 floor.
min_capital.Class A: Long-term single-parent captives maintain minimum capital and surplus at least equal to an asset-based formula, subject to a $120,000 floor.
min_capital.Class B: Long-term multi-owner captives, and long-term captives writing no more than 20 percent of net premiums from unrelated risks, maintain minimum capital and surplus at least equal to an asset-based formula, subject to a $250,000 floor.
min_capital.General-business segregated accounts and: For financial years commencing on or after 1 January 2027, each segregated account or separate account must meet the relevant solvency requirements on a stand-alone basis and must maintain capital and liquidity adequate to the risks it assumes, independently of the company's consolidated position. A segregated accounts company must not make underwriting, reserving, or distribution decisions by reference to the consolidated capital position of the company as a whole. The account is to be fully collateralised, financed up to the contract's full maximum aggregate exposure and held to the benefit of the insured, or fully funded, financed up to the reserve provision. Where the account writes fully collateralised business, the collateral must be contributed on or before the insurance contract's effective date. This guidance does not apply to long-term business. Incorporated segregated accounts are addressed separately.

tax_notes: The Insurance Act fee schedule does not impose a premium tax. Captive regulatory cost is the Bermuda Monetary Authority licence fee. The Corporate Income Tax Act 2023 charges Bermuda corporate income tax to Bermuda constituent entities of an in-scope multinational group for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. The Government of Bermuda describes that regime as its implementation of the OECD Pillar II 15 percent minimum tax for multinational groups with annual revenue of EUR 750 million or more. Captives that are not constituent entities of an in-scope group are outside that tax.
types_allowed: Class 2 multi-owner general captives and captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated net premiums
Class 3 captives writing more than 20 percent and up to 49 percent unrelated net premiums
Class B multi-owner long-term captives and long-term captives writing up to 20 percent unrelated net premiums
Segregated accounts companies and incorporated segregated accounts companies

fees.licensing_incorporation: 2026 registration fees in the Bermuda Monetary Authority fee schedule, effective 1 January 2026: Class 1 general business $2,250; Class 2 general business $4,375; Class 3 general business $17,800 where expected gross premium does not exceed $5 million, then $19,800, $22,550, $25,920, and $30,000 at the published premium bands; Class A $13,570; Class B $13,570.
fees.annual_fees: 2026 annual fees, also effective 1 January 2026, match those registration amounts for Class 1 ($2,250), Class 2 ($4,375), Class 3 ($17,800 to $30,000 by gross premium written), Class A ($13,570), and Class B ($13,570). For a segregated accounts company the premium measure combines the general account and the segregated accounts. Annual fees cancelled by deregistration, discontinuance, or merger before 31 March are pro-rated; otherwise the full annual fee is due.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax is imposed by the Insurance Act fee schedule. Bermuda corporate income tax applies only to Bermuda constituent entities of an in-scope multinational group, for fiscal years beginning on or after 1 January 2025. The Government describes the rate as the OECD Pillar II 15 percent minimum for groups with annual revenue of EUR 750 million or more.

annual_filing_requirements: Under section 17 of the Insurance Act 1978, a Class 1, Class 2, or Class 3 insurer that is not also Class C, D, or E, and a Class A or Class B insurer, files statutory financial statements within six months after the financial year-end, or within a longer period of up to nine months that the Authority allows on application. The statutory financial return under section 18 is filed at the same time. A loss-reserve specialist's opinion is required annually for a Class 3 insurer and every third year for a Class 2 insurer. The Act does not state that opinion for a Class 1 insurer. For a general-business insurer with segregated accounts or separate accounts, in a financial year commencing on or after 1 January 2027, the statutory financial statements include a Schedule of Segregated Accounts for the general account and each cell. The Schedule forms part of the annual statutory filing and is outside the scope of the statutory audit. The annual statutory submission includes a Principal Representative attestation, embedded in the Schedule and signed annually, that the Schedule reflects the position of each segregated account and the company's financial standing and that the collateral covers the associated liabilities. Under the Authority's 23 September 2026 agreed-upon procedures notice, the approved auditor performs those procedures and files the report separately from the statutory audit opinion, concurrently with the annual statutory financial return.

name: British Columbia
summary: British Columbia enacted Canada's first dedicated captive insurance statute in 1987 under the Insurance (Captive Company) Act (RSBC 1996, c. 227) and remains one of two Canadian provinces with standalone captive legislation alongside Alberta. Regulated by the BC Financial Services Authority (BCFSA), which succeeded the Financial Institutions Commission (FICOM) in 2019, it permits pure, association, and sophisticated insured captives—the latter requiring insureds to have aggregate annual insurance premiums of at least CAD 500,000. Captives can write nearly all classes of insurance or reinsurance (excluding direct surety and non-fleet automobile) and require a minimum of CAD 200,000 in shareholders' equity and CAD 100,000 in reserves. On 5 November 2026, BCFSA Statutory Approvals confirmed 20 active captives: 16 pure captives, 4 association captives, and 0 sophisticated insured captives. During 2026, 1 captive was licensed and 1 captive wound up.

name: British Virgin Islands
summary: The BVI offers a seamless approach to captive formation, leveraging a long tenure in corporate domiciliation and a deep cadre of professional expertise. It licenses various captive categories, including Category E for pure captives and segregated portfolio companies that allow independent underwriting for owners. There is no corporate income tax in the BVI, and capital requirements vary based on the insurance line.
tax_notes: No corporate income tax

name: Cayman Islands
summary: The Cayman Islands is the world's second-largest captive domicile and the leading domicile for healthcare captives, regulated by the Cayman Islands Monetary Authority (CIMA) under the Insurance Act, 2010, as amended. International insurers are licensed as Class B (B(i) where at least 95 percent of net premiums come from related business, B(ii) where more than 50 percent are related, and B(iii) where 50 percent or less are related), Class C (fully collateralised insurance-linked structures) or Class D (open-market reinsurance). As of Q3 2026, CIMA reported 720 Class B, C and D insurers, writing US$62.3 billion of premium and holding US$202.9 billion of assets. Of that population, 337 were categorised as pure captives and 149 as group captives. Medical malpractice was the primary class of 127 licensees, and North America accounted for 632 licensees (88 percent). Class B segregated portfolio companies numbered 177, with 634 segregated portfolios and 68 portfolio insurance companies; those counts sit inside the 720 and are not additional licensees. In 2025 CIMA issued 42 international licences and cancelled 19. Through the 2026 year to date, issues and cancellations were 28 and 28, leaving the international total at 720. Every captive must appoint a licensed local insurance manager. CIMA states that a complete Class B or Class C application takes six to eight weeks. The Islands levy an annual licence fee rather than a premium tax, and CIMA describes the domicile as having no corporate or personal taxes.
legislation: Insurance Act, 2010 (Law 32 of 2010), as amended, and the Insurance (Capital and Solvency) (Classes B, C and D Insurers) Regulations (2018 Revision)
applicable_legislation: Insurance Act, 2010 (Law 32 of 2010), as amended, including the Insurance (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2024 (Act 14 of 2024); Insurance (Capital and Solvency) (Classes B, C and D Insurers) Regulations (2018 Revision); Insurance (Applications and Fees) Regulations (2026 Revision), as adjusted for Class B(i), (ii) and (iii) by the Insurance (Application and Fees) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025, effective 1 January 2026; Insurance (Portfolio Insurance Companies) Regulations (2026 Revision); Companies Act (2026 Revision) segregated portfolio company provisions.

min_capital.Class B(ii) Long-term: US$300,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR

min_capital.Class B(iii) Long-term: US$400,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR
min_capital.Class B(iii) Composite: US$600,000 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement is the general-business amount plus the MCR
min_capital.Class C (general, long-term, or composit: US$500 minimum capital requirement; prescribed capital requirement equals the MCR. Obligations must be fully collateralised. CIMA may set a higher requirement from the business plan

tax_notes: No premium tax. The regulatory charge is a fixed annual licence fee under the Insurance (Applications and Fees) Regulations, as increased for Class B(i), (ii) and (iii) from 1 January 2026. CIMA states that the Cayman Islands is a tax-free domicile with no corporate or personal taxes.

Class B(ii) insurers (more than 50 percent related net premiums)
Class B(iii) insurers (50 percent or less related net premiums)

fees.licensing_incorporation: Non-refundable application fee of CI$1,000 for a Class B, C or D insurer, plus a fee on the grant of the licence equal to the annual fee. Segregated portfolio companies pay an additional CI$1,000 application amount for each segregated portfolio. US-dollar payments use CIMA's published rate of US$1.00 = CI$0.82.
fees.annual_fees: Due 15 January. From 1 January 2026: Class B(i) CI$10,450 (US$12,743.90); Class B(ii) CI$11,550 (US$14,085.37); Class B(iii) CI$14,850 (US$18,109.76); Class C CI$6,500 (US$7,926.83); Class D CI$120,000 (US$146,341.46). An SPC pays an additional CI$1,000 a year for each segregated portfolio. A portfolio insurance company pays CI$1,000 a year. A penalty of one-twelfth of the annual fee accrues for each month the fee remains outstanding.
fees.premium_tax_rate: None. Regulatory cost is the fixed annual licence fee, not a percentage of premium.

annual_filing_requirements: Annual return within six months of financial year-end, including audited financial statements prepared to internationally recognised standards by a CIMA-approved auditor, and written confirmation that the licence information remains correct. An actuarial valuation and a solvency certification are also required, except that a Class C insurer or a Class B insurer that does not write long-term business does not have to file those two items. A Class B(iii) insurer must make its audited financial statements available to insured persons and third-party beneficiaries on request. Class B, C and D insurers also file a capital and solvency return by the prescribed filing date. Annual licence fees are due by 15 January.

name: China
summary: China's captive sector is primarily focused on pure captives owned by large state-owned or private enterprises with assets exceeding RMB 100 billion. The CBIRC oversees the industry, utilizing the China Risk Oriented Solvency System (C-ROSS) without exemption for captives. There are no specific tax exemptions for captives; they are subject to standard corporate tax rates of 25% and 6% VAT.
tax_notes: 25% Corporate tax; 6% VAT

name: Connecticut
summary: Connecticut, the 'insurance capital of the world,' has modernized its captive laws and application process to offer quick decisions and a risk-based regulatory approach. The state is unique for its concentration of insurtech, commercial insurers, and experienced regulators. It offers first-year premium tax credits of $7,500 and avoids the use of outside consultants to keep formation costs low.
tax_notes: $7,500 minimum; $200,000 maximum tax

name: Cook Islands
summary: The Cook Islands enacted its Captive Insurance Act in 2013 to regulate business conducted both inside and outside its borders by international companies. As of January 2022, companies are subject to a 20% tax on worldwide income to comply with EU standards and avoid non-cooperative listing. Domicile requirements include audited annual accounts filed with the Financial Supervisory Commission.
tax_notes: 20% worldwide income tax (as of 2022)

name: Delaware
summary: Delaware licenses captives under Title 18, Chapter 69 of the Delaware Code. The Department of Insurance Bureau of Captive and Financial Insurance Products administers the chapter, and the Bureau's welcome page identifies House Bill 218 (2005) as the statute that modernized the law. The Department's 2025 year-in-review reported 638 captives after 51 new licences that year. Minimum capital and surplus is $250,000 for a pure, agency, branch or special purpose captive, $500,000 for an industrial insured captive or a sponsored captive, $750,000 for an association captive, and $1,000,000 for a risk retention group. A series captive's minimum is the amount the Commissioner specifies. Direct premium tax is 0.2 percent, with a $200,000 direct-tax cap, and assumed reinsurance premium tax is 0.1 percent, with a $110,000 cap. The annual minimum is $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive, and the annual aggregate cap is $200,000. Under § 6914(d) that premium tax is in lieu of other Delaware state and local occupation taxes, other than ad valorem property tax. A conditional certificate of authority is dated the day the Bureau receives the emailed application, if the $3,600 fee arrives within 10 business days.
legislation: Title 18, Delaware Code, Chapter 69 (Captive Insurance Companies); the Bureau identifies House Bill 218 (2005) as the modernizing statute
applicable_legislation: Title 18, Delaware Code, Chapter 69 (Captive Insurance Companies), including § 6902 (definitions), § 6903 (licence application, fees and conditional certificates), § 6905 (minimum capital and surplus), § 6906 (formation), § 6907 (annual reports), § 6914 (tax on premiums) and § 6924 (dormant captive insurance companies). The current text is published on the Delaware Code Online.

min_capital.Branch captive: USD $250,000, or such other amount as the Commissioner determines (§ 6905(a)(8))
min_capital.Special purpose captive: USD $250,000, or such other amount as the Commissioner determines (§ 6905(a)(7))
min_capital.Sponsored captive: USD $500,000 (§ 6905(a)(6)). This is the sponsored captive minimum, not a published per-cell floor
min_capital.Special purpose financial captive: USD $500,000 if it is also a sponsored captive; USD $250,000 if it is not (§ 6905(a)(9))
min_capital.Series captive: The amount specified by the Commissioner (§ 6905(a)(10)). No default dollar amount is published in the statute
min_capital.Additional and form of capital: The Commissioner may prescribe additional capital and surplus based on the type, volume and nature of the business (§ 6905(b)). Minimum capital is held as cash, an irrevocable letter of credit from an institution chartered, licensed or otherwise authorized to do banking business in Delaware, or another institution or asset the Commissioner approves. Surplus-note proceeds may count if the Commissioner approves the note (§ 6905(c) and (d))

tax_notes: Direct premiums are taxed at 2/10 of 1 percent (0.2 percent), up to $200,000, and assumed reinsurance premiums at 1/10 of 1 percent (0.1 percent), up to $110,000. Premiums already taxed as direct premiums are not taxed again as assumed reinsurance, and no tax is due on annuity consideration. The annual minimum aggregate tax is $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive. The annual maximum aggregate tax is $200,000, except that series captives formed in the same limited liability company or statutory trust are not aggregated into that cap. A captive that employs at least 25 qualified full-time individuals in Delaware pays $50,000 if the formula would otherwise exceed that amount. Tax is due by 15 April. Under § 6914(d) this premium tax is all of the tax collectible under Delaware law from a captive, and no other occupation tax is levied by the State or by a county, city or municipality, except ad valorem taxes on real and personal property used in the production of income. A dormant captive is not liable for the premium tax. There is no separate Delaware corporate income tax on captives in Chapter 69.
contact_name: Stephen Taylor, Director, Bureau of Captive & Financial Insurance Products

fees.licensing_incorporation: Nonrefundable application fee of $300 to review completeness, plus a nonrefundable processing fee of $3,200 (18 Del. C. § 6903(d)). The 2024 Bureau application notice collects $3,500 for a regular application. A conditional certificate adds a $100 fee under § 6903(d)(5); the same 2024 notice collects $3,600 for a conditional application. The annual licence fee for the year of registration is $400.
fees.annual_fees: $400 certificate-of-authority renewal fee, due 15 April, payable with the premium-tax report. From the 2025 premium tax and 2026 renewal, payment may be made through OPTins or by the existing procedure. A dormant captive that has not resumed business after five years pays a renewal fee of $25,000 in the sixth year of dormancy and $5,000 in each year of dormancy after that (§ 6924(g)).
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums 0.2 percent, maximum $200,000. Assumed reinsurance premiums 0.1 percent, maximum $110,000. Annual minimum aggregate tax $5,000, or $3,500 for a series captive. Annual maximum aggregate tax $200,000. A captive with at least 25 qualified Delaware employees is capped at $50,000. No annuity tax. Dormant captives pay no premium tax.

annual_filing_requirements: Each captive other than a branch captive for which the Commissioner has waived the requirement files a report of financial condition by 15 April, verified by oath of two executive officers or authorized persons, using GAAP unless the Commissioner approves statutory accounting principles or international accounting standards (§ 6907). The Bureau requires the annual report (Form F-1, updated 31 March 2025, for pure captives, core LLCs and series; special purpose financial captives that file NAIC statements are excepted) by 15 April, or within 60 days of fiscal year-end where an alternate year-end is used. Audited financial statements and a statement of actuarial opinion, for captives that retain risk, are due by 30 June. Special purpose financial captives also file quarterly reports with the NAIC and the Bureau by 15 May, 15 August and 15 November. Premium tax and the $400 renewal fee are due by 15 April. Annual reports are emailed to captive@delaware.gov.

licensing_speed: The 2024 Bureau application notice dates a conditional certificate on the day the emailed application is received, provided the $3,600 fee reaches the Dover accounting office within 10 business days. Only a captive manager that already manages at least two Delaware captives may file a conditional application. In October 2023 the Department said its goal for review of initial application filings is 30 days, down from 45, and that conditional applications received after 1 November are reviewed within 80 days. That 2023 goal is not restated in the 2024 notice or the March 2026 OPTins notice.

name: District of Columbia
summary: The District of Columbia licenses captives under the Captive Insurance Company Act of 2004, Chapter 39A of Title 31 of the D.C. Code, administered by the Department of Insurance, Securities and Banking Risk Finance Bureau. The 2000 captive law was repealed and replaced by that Act. The first captive was licensed in 2001. A captive may be a pure, association, agency, rental, branch, or protected-cell captive, and a risk retention group may be licensed as a captive. Any type of captive may form protected cells, including incorporated cells that are separate legal entities. Special purpose financial captives are authorized in Subchapter II. A wildcard provision lets the Commissioner authorize a qualified captive to engage in any activity permitted for a captive in any other jurisdiction. On 30 October 2025 the Bureau reported 215 active risk-bearing entities: 49 pure, including 6 protected-cell-captive cores; 10 association captives that are not risk retention groups, including 3 protected-cell-captive cores; 1 agency protected-cell captive; 4 branch captives; 16 rental captives, all protected-cell captives; 29 risk retention groups; and 106 protected cells, of which 78 were unincorporated and 28 were incorporated. Through that date in 2025 the Bureau had licensed 23 entities: 1 incorporated cell, 20 unincorporated protected cells, and 2 risk retention groups. It also said 413 captives had been licensed since 2001. The same presentation reported 2024 captive assets of $11,396,881,785 and 2024 gross written premium of $2,954,868,515. DISB also posts a licensed-captives roster dated 14 July 2026. That roster does not state a total, so the 30 October 2025 census is the figure stored here. A captive other than a protected-cell captive maintains at least $100,000 of unimpaired capital. Unencumbered surplus is at least $150,000 for a pure captive, $300,000 for an agency captive, a rental captive, or a stock association captive, and $500,000 for a mutual or reciprocal association captive. The Commissioner sets cell capital and surplus, and the Bureau's 30 October 2025 presentation states that the minimum is $0 for a protected-cell captive and $0 for cells, including incorporated cells. Non-risk-retention-group direct premium tax starts at 0.25 percent on the first $25 million, with a $7,500 minimum and a $100,000 maximum. The application review fee is $500 and the certificate-of-authority fee is $300, renewed annually by 30 April. Properly documented applications are processed within 30 days. The Bureau page still displays Dana Sheppard as Associate Commissioner for Risk Finance. The 30 October 2025 presentation lists her as Deputy Commissioner for Market Operations and lists Sean O'Donnell as Associate Commissioner, and the Bureau's 7 November 2025 and 17 December 2025 notices are issued by Sean O'Donnell in that office. No dormant-captive statute is in force. The October 2025 presentation said a proposal to add one had been submitted and that no significant captive law had passed in 2025.
legislation: Captive Insurance Company Act of 2004, D.C. Code Title 31, Chapter 39A
applicable_legislation: D.C. Code Title 31, Chapter 39A, Subchapter I, enacted as D.C. Law 15-262 (17 March 2005) and amended since, including the Captive Insurance Company Amendment Act of 2014, D.C. Law 20-203. Chapter 39, the 2000 captive law, is repealed by section 31-3931.23. Capital and surplus are section 31-3931.06. Protected cells are section 31-3931.04. Premium tax is section 31-3931.12. The annual report is section 31-3931.13. Financial examination is section 31-3931.14. Certificate-of-authority renewal by 30 April is section 31-3931.09(d), as cited in the Bureau's 2025 reporting instructions. Special purpose financial captive capital is section 31-3932.05. Non-risk-retention-group audit timing is also in 26 DCMR section 3702, as cited by the Bureau.

min_capital.Captive other than a protected cell capt: At least $100,000 of minimum unimpaired capital, in addition to any further capital the Commissioner requires (D.C. Code section 31-3931.06(a)(1)).
min_capital.Pure captive: At least $150,000 of unencumbered surplus, in addition to required capital (section 31-3931.06(f)(1)).
min_capital.Protected cell captive and each protecte: The Commissioner sets the minimum capital and the minimum surplus for the protected cell captive and for each cell. Protected-cell-captive capital may be zero if each cell maintains the capital required for that cell. A protected cell captive that does not write insurance business in the District is not required to maintain surplus if each cell maintains the surplus required for that cell (section 31-3931.06(a)(2) and (f)(6)). The Bureau's 30 October 2025 presentation states the minimum as $0 for protected cell captives and $0 for cells, including incorporated cells.
min_capital.Special purpose financial captive: At least $100,000 of unimpaired capital and at least $150,000 of unencumbered surplus (section 31-3932.05(a) and (e)).
min_capital.Risk retention group: Section 31-3931.06(l) applies section 31-2502.12 to a risk retention group licensed as a captive. The captive surplus schedule does not state a separate risk-retention-group dollar floor, and no separate floor is restated here.
min_capital.Form of capital and surplus: Cash or an irrevocable letter of credit, unless the Commissioner provides otherwise. The letter of credit is issued by a District-chartered bank, or a District branch of a Federal Reserve member bank or an FDIC-insured bank, on a form the Commissioner approves, and it renews automatically each year.

tax_notes: Section 31-3931.12 requires premium tax by 2 March. For a captive that is not a risk retention group, net direct premiums are taxed at 0.250 percent on the first $25 million, 0.150 percent on the next $25 million, and 0.050 percent thereafter. A risk retention group pays 0.38 percent on the first $20 million of total net direct premiums, 0.25 percent on the next $20 million, and 0.18 percent thereafter. Assumed-reinsurance premiums are taxed at 0.225 percent on the first $25 million, 0.150 percent on the next $25 million, and 0.025 percent thereafter. Reinsurance tax is not levied on risks already taxed as direct premiums, or on a qualifying assumption of loss reserves from an insurer under common ownership and control that is being discontinued. A captive other than a risk retention group licensed as an association captive pays at least $7,500. A risk retention group licensed as an association captive pays at least $15,000. The total tax does not exceed $100,000 in any year. Annuity business is not taxed. Branch tax applies only to branch business. A captive licensed in the last quarter of the calendar year may ask the Commissioner to reduce the minimum. The tax is in lieu of other District taxes except real property tax and personal property tax. The Bureau's 2025 reporting instructions say each protected cell captive and each incorporated cell files a separate premium-tax return, incorporated cells are subject to the $7,500 minimum, unincorporated protected cells file a consolidated return with the protected cell captive, and each unincorporated protected cell is not subject to the minimum. From 1 January 2026, premium tax and certificate-of-authority renewal payments are made through NAIC OPTins. The NAIC charges $17.50 per OPTins transaction.
contact_name: Sean O'Donnell, Associate Commissioner, Risk Finance Bureau
types_allowed: Incorporated protected cells and unincorporated protected cells
Risk retention groups licensed as captive insurers
Special purpose financial captive insurance companies

fees.licensing_incorporation: The forming page and the Bureau's 30 October 2025 presentation require a $500 application review fee and a $300 certificate-of-authority fee with the application. Incorporation is handled inside the Department. The presentation states that there are no fees other than the $500 application fee, the $300 annual certificate-of-authority fee, and annual premium taxes. Section 31-3931.04(b)(4) also says a protected cell captive pays an additional annual fee for each protected cell in an amount the Commissioner establishes. No separate dollar amount for that cell fee was published on the pages reviewed. A certification of captive documents is $10, paid in advance, under the Bureau's certification-fee notice.
fees.annual_fees: Annual certificate-of-authority renewal fee of $300, due on or before 30 April under section 31-3931.09(d), as stated in the 17 December 2025 reporting instructions. Beginning with the 2026-2027 renewals, renewal payments are made through NAIC OPTins. The NAIC charges $17.50 per transaction. The Commissioner may fine, suspend, or revoke a certificate that is not renewed by 1 August.
fees.premium_tax_rate: Non-risk-retention-group direct premiums: 0.25 percent on the first $25 million, 0.15 percent on the next $25 million, and 0.05 percent thereafter. Risk-retention-group direct premiums: 0.38 percent, 0.25 percent, and 0.18 percent on successive $20 million bands. Assumed reinsurance: 0.225 percent, 0.150 percent, and 0.025 percent on successive $25 million bands. Minimum $7,500, or $15,000 for a risk retention group licensed as an association captive. Maximum $100,000. Due 2 March. Incorporated cells owe the $7,500 minimum. An unincorporated protected cell is not separately subject to the minimum.

annual_filing_requirements: On or before 2 March, a captive, including each protected cell, submits a report of its financial condition prepared by a certified public accountant. Reporting uses generally accepted accounting principles unless the Commissioner accepts modifications. A protected cell captive files a consolidated report for its cells, and the 2025 instructions also require separate unaudited DC blanks for the protected cell captive, each incorporated cell, and each unincorporated protected cell. A pure captive may be allowed to report on its parent's fiscal year, with the report due within 60 days after fiscal year-end, and it still files premium-tax support by 2 March. Risk retention groups also comply with Chapter 3 of Title 31 and file the actuarial opinion by 2 March and the actuarial opinion summary by 15 March. Non-risk-retention-group audited financial reports are due 30 June under 26 DCMR section 3702. Risk-retention-group audits are due 1 June. Combined cell audits and combined actuarial opinions, when used, are due 30 June. A branch captive files copies of the reports its parent files at home, certified by two officers, plus a branch premium and reserve statement. For a 31 December branch, those filings are due 30 June. Premium tax is due 2 March. The certificate of authority is renewed by 30 April. Financial filings are emailed to captive.filings@dc.gov. From 1 January 2026, premium tax and renewal payments go through OPTins. The board meets at least once each year in the District. The Bureau's one-pager states that the meeting may be held by teleconference or webcast and that a local director is not required. The captive maintains an office in the District. Examinations are at the Commissioner's discretion and at the captive's cost. The Commissioner may waive the five-year examination in Chapter 14 for a captive that is not a risk retention group, has filed unqualified audits, has sufficient surplus, and is in compliance. The 30 October 2025 presentation describes non-risk-retention-group supervision as an annual desk analysis, with examinations at the regulator's discretion. No dormant-captive filing regime is in the current statute.

name: Dubai
summary: The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) is a leading hub for the MEASA region, connecting emerging markets with a proven judicial system and an English common law framework. Regulated by the independent DFSA, the domicile offers 100% digital onboarding and a 0% tax rate on corporate income guaranteed until 2054. It allows for pure, third-party, and association captives with case-by-case flexibility on capital structures.
tax_notes: 0% tax until 2054; waived commercial license fees

name: Federated States of Micronesia
summary: Micronesia enacted its captive law in 2006 specifically to provide Japanese corporations with a conveniently located domicile under a responsive regulatory environment. Captives are required to file audited financial statements that can be prepared under US or Japanese GAAP. Beyond a low 0.05% premium tax, captives also file a simple annual income tax return computed at 21% of net income.
tax_notes: 0.05% premium tax; 21% net income tax

name: Florida
summary: Florida's captive provisions were augmented in 2012 to further specify criteria for formation, capital, and licensure. The state's unique selling point is its relatively low capital requirements across its four main captive types: pure, industrial insured, special purpose, and reinsurance. Interested parties are directed to Chapter 628 of the Florida statutes for detailed variation in requirement by captive type.
tax_notes: Requires annual reporting compliance

name: France
summary: France is a growing challenger in the European market, applying Solvency II regulations to ensure high quality in shareholders and solvency. Domiciling in France allows direct captives to operate across Europe under the Freedom of Service principle. The regulator, ACPR, maintains a dedicated team for captive supervision and emphasizes solid governance structured around '4 eyes' principles.
tax_notes: Freedom of Service access across the EU

name: Georgia
summary: Georgia licenses captive insurance companies under the Georgia Captive Insurance Company Act, Chapter 41 of Title 33, enacted in 1988 and administered by the Captives Division of the Office of the Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire. The chapter covers pure, association, agency, industrial insured, and sponsored captives, and risk retention group captives. A sponsored captive may use incorporated or unincorporated protected cells. House Bill 348, effective 1 June 2025, amended the permissible-business section so that a captive may engage in any insurance or reinsurance the Commissioner deems reasonable, still subject to the ownership and risk limits in O.C.G.A. section 33-41-3. Workers' compensation and motor-vehicle policies must meet Georgia's minimum coverage requirements. Surplus floors are $250,000 for a pure, agency, or sponsored captive and $500,000 for an association captive, an industrial insured captive, or a risk retention group. A dormant captive maintains at least $25,000. Direct premium tax is 0.4 percent on the first $20 million and 0.3 percent thereafter. Assumed-reinsurance premium tax runs from 0.225 percent down to 0.025 percent across $20 million bands. The annual maximum is $100,000. The statute does not state a minimum premium tax. The license fee is $600 at application and the renewal fee is $500 each later year. The Division's formation page says proposed articles are approved or disapproved within 45 days and the certificate of authority within 90 days, with a further 90-day extension available under O.C.G.A. section 33-3-15. The Captives Division contact page publishes captivedivision@oci.ga.gov and does not name a captive program head or a section headcount. The Division pages reviewed do not publish a current captive census.
legislation: Georgia Captive Insurance Company Act, O.C.G.A. Title 33, Chapter 41, and Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Chapter 120-2-45
applicable_legislation: O.C.G.A. Title 33, Chapter 41, Article 1, enacted by Ga. L. 1988, p. 966, and Article 2 on sponsored captive insurance companies, enacted in 2019. House Bill 348, Act 258, effective 1 June 2025, amended sections 33-41-2 and 33-41-3. Capital and surplus are section 33-41-8. Premium tax is section 33-41-22. Reports are section 33-41-15. Examinations are section 33-41-16. The certificate of dormancy is section 33-41-23. License and renewal fees are Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. Rule 120-2-45-.12. Annual statements are Rule 120-2-45-.07. Audits are Rule 120-2-45-.09. Examinations and the organizational-examination fee are Rule 120-2-45-.08. Premium-tax filing is Rule 120-2-45-.13.

min_capital.Pure captive: At least $250,000 in surplus. The Commissioner sets the amount individually and may require more based on the business plan (O.C.G.A. section 33-41-8(a)(1)).
min_capital.Sponsored captive: At least $250,000 in surplus under section 33-41-8(a)(6), and at least $250,000 in capital and surplus under section 33-41-101(9)(B), available to pay expenses and claims of the sponsored captive. Article 2 does not state a separate dollar floor for an unincorporated protected cell.
min_capital.Dormant captive: At least $25,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus while a certificate of dormancy is in force. If the Commissioner allows dormancy while liabilities remain, the Commissioner may require more capital, surplus, and reserves (section 33-41-23).
min_capital.Form and deposit: Minimum capital or surplus of up to $500,000 is held in cash, FDIC-insured certificates of deposit, insured savings accounts or certificates, or letters of credit that meet section 33-41-9. Additional capital above $500,000 may be held in eligible investments under section 33-11-5, shareholder obligations secured by letters of credit, or other investments the Commissioner approves. An association captive, an industrial insured captive, and a risk retention group must deposit with the state before the certificate of authority is issued. The current text of section 33-41-8(c) requires that deposit and does not state its dollar amount.

tax_notes: O.C.G.A. section 33-41-22 imposes the captive tax in lieu of any other taxes imposed by Title 33. Direct premiums, after return premiums and policyholder dividends or premium deposits returned or credited, are taxed at 0.4 percent on the first $20 million and 0.3 percent on each dollar thereafter. A risk retention group captive is subject to that direct-premium tax only on coverages within Georgia. Assumed-reinsurance premium is taxed at 0.225 percent on the first $20 million, 0.150 percent on the next $20 million, 0.050 percent on the next $20 million, and 0.025 percent thereafter. Reinsurance tax does not apply to risks taxed on a direct basis, or to a qualifying assumption of loss reserves and other liabilities of another insurer under common ownership and control that the Commissioner verifies is part of a plan to discontinue that insurer. If the calculated tax exceeds $100,000 in a year, the tax is $100,000. The section does not state a minimum tax. Two or more captives under common ownership and control, other than sponsored captives, are taxed as one captive. Common ownership and control means more than 50 percent of the voting securities or membership interests. A protected cell is a captive for this tax. The aggregation rule applies to each cell and its participants, and the sponsored captive collects and remits the cells' tax. The annual return and payment are due 1 March under Rule 120-2-45-.13. A late return or payment draws a $5,000 penalty. An extension of not more than 30 days may be granted, with interest of 1 percent per month. Rule 120-2-45-.13(3) says a risk retention group files and pays premium tax under O.C.G.A. section 33-40-5. A separate section 33-40-5 rate is not restated here. A dormant captive that holds a certificate of dormancy is not liable for the section 33-41-22 tax. No Georgia corporate income-tax rate for captives is stated in Chapter 41.

fees.licensing_incorporation: Rule 120-2-45-.12 requires a $600 license fee when the application for a certificate of authority is filed. If the Commissioner requires an organizational examination, Rule 120-2-45-.08 requires $3,000 payable to the appointed examiner, and the Commissioner may require a higher amount in writing. O.C.G.A. section 33-41-10(c) also requires the applicant to pay the costs of examining, investigating, and processing the original or renewal application. Corporate formation fees payable to the Georgia Secretary of State are not set in Chapter 41.
fees.annual_fees: A renewal fee of $500 is due for each year after the initial year of licensure (Rule 120-2-45-.12). A certificate of dormancy is renewed every five years for $500 (O.C.G.A. section 33-41-23(b)(3)).
fees.premium_tax_rate: Direct premiums: 0.4 percent on the first $20 million and 0.3 percent thereafter. A risk retention group is taxed under section 33-41-22 only on direct premiums for Georgia coverages, and Rule 120-2-45-.13(3) points risk-retention-group premium-tax filing to O.C.G.A. section 33-40-5. Assumed reinsurance: 0.225 percent, 0.150 percent, 0.050 percent, and 0.025 percent on successive $20 million bands. No minimum is stated in section 33-41-22. Annual maximum $100,000. Due 1 March. Late filing or payment penalty $5,000.

annual_filing_requirements: Each captive files the reports of its business affairs required by O.C.G.A. section 33-3-21, as section 33-41-15 provides. Rule 120-2-45-.07 requires, on or before 1 March, a report of financial condition as of the preceding 31 December, verified by the oath of an executive officer. A pure captive elects generally accepted accounting principles or statutory accounting principles. An industrial insured captive and an association captive use statutory accounting principles. An industrial insured captive, an association captive, and a risk retention group file the NAIC property-and-casualty blank by 1 March. An industrial insured or association captive that directly writes workers' compensation, and every risk retention group, also files quarterly NAIC blanks as of 31 March, 30 June, and 30 September, due 15 May, 15 August, and 15 November. Rule 120-2-45-.09 requires an audited financial report by 30 June. The audit includes an opinion on the adequacy of loss and loss-expense reserves by a Fellow of the Casualty Actuarial Society, a member of the American Academy of Actuaries, or another person who has demonstrated competence in loss-reserve evaluation and whom the Commissioner approves. The premium-tax return is due 1 March. A sponsored captive's annual financial report includes the financial experience of each protected cell. The Commissioner may examine a captive at any time, and Rule 120-2-45-.08 says an examination occurs no less often than once every five years unless the Commissioner makes a written finding that a longer period is warranted. At least one director or manager is a Georgia resident, and the company reports a director or manager change within 30 days. A material change that is not disapproved within 30 days after submission is deemed approved. A dormant captive files a financial-condition report by 1 March and does not file the other annual forms, fees, or documents that Chapter 41 would otherwise require. Filings and payments are submitted through the GIMS portal.

name: Germany
summary: While not a typical domicile, Germany attracts captives through compliance requirements and the efficiency of sharing staff with parent companies and in-house brokers. Operations are governed by Solvency II and Section 122 VAG, with BaFin withdrawing authorization if eligible funds fall below strict minimums. Minimum capital requirements are calculated based on EU Delegated Regulation 2015/35.
tax_notes: No specific tax exemptions reported

name: Gibraltar
summary: As an onshore domicile for over 50 years, Gibraltar offers captive owners direct access to the UK market under flexible EU-based laws. It features a low flat tax rate of 10% which has been in effect since 2010. While capital requirements can be more onerous than offshore locations, the domicile permits varied structures including protected cell companies and managing general agents.

min_capital.General: More onerous than offshore; varies by structure

tax_notes: 10% across the board tax rate

name: Guam
summary: Guam offers a unique geographical advantage for US-linked business in the Pacific and features 100% tax abatement and rebates for corporate and gross receipts taxes. Legislation enacted in 1996 and subsequent amendments provide an attractive environment for risk management headquarters. Capital and surplus can be held in cash or irrevocable letters of credit approved by the commissioner.
tax_notes: 100% tax rebates for commercial and captive companies

name: Guernsey
summary: Guernsey is a leading captive centre and the jurisdiction that pioneered the protected cell company. The Guernsey Financial Services Commission regulates insurers under the Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, using its own solvency rules rather than the EU Solvency II standard formula. At 31 December 2025 the Commission reported 196 non-cellular captives, after 8 additions and 9 surrenders in 2025. That 196 is not a total of all captives: of cells reported by type of insurer, 126 were classified as captives, after 13 additions and 9 surrenders. Pure/single-parent and group/association captive structures are permitted; the Commission does not publish a numerical breakdown of those types, a captive-only premium total, or a standard licensing time. At 31 December 2025 the international insurance sector comprised 44 PCCs, 222 PCC cells excluding insurance-linked securities, 14 ICCs and 46 ICC cells. Those PCC and ICC totals cover the wider international insurance sector and are not all captives. The same sector statistics also show 223 companies and 549 entities in total. The latest financial totals, for 2024, were £29.70 billion of gross assets, £12.62 billion of net worth and £5.19 billion of premiums written by international insurers as a whole, not by captives alone. Captive (re)insurers are Category 5 licensees. Category 6, including special purpose insurers and insurance-linked securities, is authorised separately and is not necessarily captive business. The capital floor is £100,000 for general business and £250,000 for long-term business, and the captive prescribed capital requirement is calibrated at a 90 percent confidence level over 12 months. Under the Income Tax (Guernsey) Law, 1975, as amended, and States of Guernsey Revenue Service guidance, company income tax is 0 percent on insurance income that is not domestic business and 10 percent on domestic insurance business. Reinsurance is outside the statutory definition of domestic business. Insurance supervision is carried out by the Banking and Insurance Division; the Commission does not publish a separate current headcount for insurance supervision alone. The Commission regulates insurers and does not administer individual captives. Most international insurers are administered by licensed insurance managers: 23 were authorised at 31 December 2025, and named managers are on the regulated-entities register. The Commission can pre-authorise later protected-cell-company cells on a product or class basis once the company and its first cell are approved, most often for fully collateralised special purpose insurer cells. It does not publish a 48-hour licensing standard. This profile was reviewed by the Commission (Shaun Green, 5 November 2026) against its published insurance statistics.

min_capital.Category 5 captive, general business: £100,000 capital floor. Paid-up share capital must be at least the capital floor, and minimum shareholders' funds must be at least 75 percent of the capital floor. The minimum capital requirement cannot be below the capital floor. The prescribed capital requirement is set at a 90 percent confidence level over the next 12 months
min_capital.Category 5 captive, long-term business: £250,000 capital floor, with the same paid-up capital, shareholders' funds and 90 percent prescribed-capital tests
min_capital.Protected cell company that does not wri: The capital floor applies to the PCC as a whole. There is no separate capital floor for each cell or for the core. Each cell and the core has a notional minimum capital requirement calculated as if it were a stand-alone insurer, and the PCC minimum is the sum of those amounts, subject to the capital floor

The 10 percent company intermediate rate applies to income from domestic insurance business, insurance intermediary business and insurance manager business. Insurance income that is not domestic business, including reinsurance (which the Insurance Business (Bailiwick of Guernsey) Law, 2002, as amended, excludes from domestic business), is taxed at 0 percent. Income from Guernsey land and buildings is taxed at 20 percent. Insurance is an economic-substance category for accounting periods after 1 January 2019. Revenue Service company-tax guidance does not state a separate premium-tax rate.

The general representative is responsible for filing. A late return attracts an administrative financial penalty. Licensed insurance managers and insurance intermediaries deposit their annual return within six months of the financial year-end. Guernsey company income tax returns are filed separately with the Revenue Service; the 2025 corporate return is due 30 November 2026.

name: Hawaii
summary: Hawaii has licensed captive insurers since May 1986 under Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 431, Article 19, administered by the Insurance Division's Captive Insurance Branch. The Hawaii Insurance Division, regulator correspondence, November 2026, reported 269 captives at year-end 2025 and 276 captive companies as of 30 September 2026, after 14 formations and 7 surrenders or dissolutions in 2026 through that date. Those movements reconcile the year-end count with the September census. Of the 276, Class 1 accounted for 28, Class 2 for 194, pre-class structures for 19, Class 3 for 14, Class 4 for 12, and Class 5 for 9. The Captive Insurance Branch has 16 staff, and a typical licence takes about 30 days. Licenses are issued in five classes. The statutory floors for unimpaired capital and surplus are $100,000 for a Class 1 pure captive that reinsures only, $250,000 for a Class 2 pure captive that may write direct insurance, and $500,000 for a Class 3 association or risk retention captive and for a Class 4 sponsored captive. Class 5 reinsurance or excess captives, and the security a branch captive posts in Hawaii, are set by the Insurance Commissioner. Premium tax has no minimum and a $200,000 maximum, and it does not apply to premiums already taxed where the risk is located or to reinsurance premiums assumed by the captive. A dormant captive holding a certificate of dormancy maintains at least $25,000 of capital and surplus and is not subject to that tax.
legislation: Hawaii Revised Statutes Chapter 431, Article 19 (Captive Insurance Companies)
applicable_legislation: Hawaii Revised Statutes Title 24, Chapter 431, Article 19 (Captive Insurance Companies), including §431:19-101 (classes), §431:19-102 (certificate of authority), §431:19-104 (minimum capital and surplus), §431:19-107 (financial statements), §431:19-108 (examinations), §431:19-116 (taxation), and §431:19-117 (dormant captive insurance companies, added by Act 69, Session Laws of Hawaii 2024). License and application fees are set in Hawaii Administrative Rules §16-17-6.

min_capital.Class 1: Not less than $100,000. A Class 1 company is a pure captive licensed to write business only as a reinsurer (HRS §§431:19-101 and 431:19-104).
min_capital.Class 2: Not less than $250,000. A Class 2 company is a pure captive licensed to write direct insurance, or direct insurance and reinsurance.
min_capital.Class 3: Not less than $500,000. A Class 3 company is an association captive or a risk retention captive. Other provisions of Chapter 431 may require more.
min_capital.Class 4: Not less than $500,000. A Class 4 company is a sponsored captive.
min_capital.Class 5: An amount set by the Insurance Commissioner case by case. A Class 5 company is a reinsurance or excess captive licensed under HRS §431:19-111.5.
min_capital.Branch captive: In lieu of the class minimum, the commissioner determines the amount and form of security maintained in Hawaii after considering the risk retained in the state, the outside captive's financial condition, and other security already posted (HRS §431:19-104(c)).
min_capital.Dormant captive: Not less than $25,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus while a certificate of dormancy is in force (HRS §431:19-117).
min_capital.Commissioner discretion: The commissioner sets each captive's required unimpaired capital and surplus after considering the nature and volume of its business. The class amounts are floors. Capital may be held in cash, an irrevocable letter of credit, public obligations, or another form the commissioner approves.

tax_notes: Premium tax under HRS §431:19-116 is paid to the director of finance through the commissioner by March 1. On gross premiums for risks resident, situated, or located in Hawaii, and on risks elsewhere on which no premium tax is otherwise paid, less return premiums and less reinsurance accepted, the rates are 0.25% from $0 to $25 million, 0.15% from more than $25 million to $50 million, 0.05% from more than $50 million to $250 million, and 0% above $250 million. There is no minimum tax. The annual maximum aggregate tax is $200,000. The tax is in lieu of other Hawaii state and county taxes except taxes on real property and on the purchase, use, or ownership of tangible personal property. The Insurance Division states the same rule as a tax on the captive's own premiums only, with no tax on premiums already taxed where the underlying risk is located and no tax on reinsurance premiums assumed by the captive. A dormant captive that holds a certificate of dormancy is not subject to the §431:19-116 tax (HRS §431:19-117).

fees.licensing_incorporation: $50 initial business-registration incorporation fee and a $1,000 nonrefundable captive application fee. If the commissioner uses an independent advisor to review an application or business-plan amendment, the applicant pays a reasonable fee authorized by the commissioner (HRS §431:19-102; Hawaii Administrative Rules §16-17-6).
fees.annual_fees: $15 annual business-registration fee. The certificate-of-authority renewal, due on or before April 1, is $300 for a Class 1 or Class 2 captive, $500 for a Class 3 captive, and $1,000 for a Class 4 or Class 5 captive (HAR §16-17-6). A certificate of dormancy is renewed every five years for $300 (HRS §431:19-117).
fees.premium_tax_rate: 0.25% on the first $25 million, 0.15% from $25 million to $50 million, 0.05% from $50 million to $250 million, and 0% above $250 million. No minimum tax. Maximum annual tax $200,000. No tax on premiums already taxed where the risk is located, on assumed reinsurance, or on a dormant captive holding a certificate of dormancy.

annual_filing_requirements: A captive other than a risk retention captive files financial statements, prepared on generally accepted accounting principles or another basis the commissioner accepts and audited by an independent certified public accountant or another professional the commissioner accepts, on or before the last day of the sixth month after its fiscal year-end (HRS §431:19-107(a)). A risk retention captive files an NAIC annual statement and a risk-based capital report by March 1 and an audit by June 1. Actuarial opinions on reserves are included with the audited statements, except that a Class 3 company files its actuarial opinion with the annual statement by March 1. The premium-tax statement is due March 1 (HRS §431:19-116). The governing body holds at least one meeting each year in Hawaii, and the captive keeps its principal place of business in the state (HRS §431:19-102). Examinations occur at least once every five years; a risk retention captive is examined no later than three years after formation and at least once every five years after that (HRS §431:19-108). The Captive Insurance Branch requires electronic annual filings to CaptiveInsAnnualFilings@dcca.hawaii.gov. A dormant captive with a certificate of dormancy files a verified report of its financial condition by March 1 and does not file the audited statements required by §431:19-107.

name: Hong Kong

name: Illinois
summary: Illinois modernized its Insurance Code in 2018 to lower capital and surplus requirements and filing fees, making the state a more viable captive domicile. The state now allows captives to make loans to affiliates with prior approval and permits captive reinsurance pools. Despite having one of the highest GDPs in the US, Illinois has only recently become an active competitor in the captive space.
tax_notes: $2,000 filing fee (lowered from $7,000)

name: Ireland
summary: Ireland is a global re/insurance center that provides a stable operating environment with direct access to all EEA countries through EU passporting. The Central Bank of Ireland (CBI) applies Solvency II proportionately through its PRISM system, which allows captives to have fewer directors and less frequent meetings. The state is also known for managing non-traditional risks like employee benefits.

min_capital.Requirement: Adheres to EU Solvency II framework

tax_notes: Transparent tax regime; Freedom of Service (FoS) access

name: Isle of Man
summary: The Isle of Man Financial Services Authority licenses captives as Class 12 insurers under the Insurance Act 2008 and the Insurance Regulations 2025, in operation from 30 June 2025. A Class 12 insurer may insure its own group, connected entities and connected individuals, and may reinsure a related customer only where a qualifying ceding insurer remains liable for the underlying claim. At 31 March 2025 the Authority reported 81 authorised Class 12 insurers. For non-life Class 12 business the minimum capital requirement is the higher of 75 percent of the solvency capital requirement and £100,000, and the fixed floor is £0 for a protected-cell-company cell. The solvency capital requirement for a non-dormant Class 12 insurer is a one-year value-at-risk at a 90 percent confidence level. The standard rate of Isle of Man corporate income tax is 0 percent. From 1 April 2026 the annual fee for a Class 12 authorised insurer is £8,565. A draft Class 12 and Class 13 valuation framework, consulted on in CP26-01, is written to come into operation on 31 December 2026 and is not in force.
