name: Texas
summary: Texas licenses captive insurance companies under Insurance Code Chapter 964, added in 2013 by Senate Bill 734 and effective 14 June 2013. A 2017 amendment authorized captive exchanges. A captive may write direct insurance and reinsurance, but only for the operational risks of its affiliates and the risks of a controlled unaffiliated business. It may be formed in any form of organization authorized by the Business Organizations Code except a risk retention group or a general partnership, and it may be a nonprofit corporation only if a nonprofit corporation controls it. A captive exchange is a reciprocal or interinsurance exchange and operates as a captive insurance company. The commissioner sets unencumbered capital and surplus, or the equivalent, at not less than $250,000. Premium tax under Chapter 223A is one-half of one percent of taxable premium receipts, with a $7,500 annual minimum and a $200,000 annual maximum. Premiums received from another authorized insurer for reinsurance are not taxed, and there is no deduction for premiums paid for reinsurance. Captives also pay the insurance maintenance tax on correctly reported gross premiums from risks located in Texas. The application fee is $1,500. Affiliates must have significant operations in Texas, the governing body meets at least once a year in the state, and the principal office and books and records stay in Texas unless the commissioner approves a move. TDI's 15 April 2026 post reported that the sector grew 8.6 percent to 101 state-domiciled captives in the six months leading up to April 2026, and quoted the captive specialist that Texas has only one type of captive. The fiscal 2025 annual report counted 93 captive insurance company licenses. No formation, surrender, or type split was published with the figure of 101.
legislation: Texas Insurance Code Chapter 964 (Captive Insurance Companies) and Chapter 223A (Captive Insurance Premium Tax)
applicable_legislation: Texas Insurance Code Chapter 964, added by Acts 2013, 83rd Legislature, Regular Session, Chapter 569 (Senate Bill 734), effective 14 June 2013, and amended by Acts 2017, 85th Legislature, Regular Session, Chapter 1050 (House Bill 1944), effective 15 June 2017, including the captive-exchange subchapter. Capital and surplus are section 964.056. The application and the $1,500 application fee are section 964.057. The annual report is section 964.060. The maintenance tax is section 964.068. Premium tax is Chapter 223A, added by the same 2013 act. Captive administrative rules are Title 28, Texas Administrative Code, Chapter 6. The Comptroller's captive premium-tax rule is 34 Texas Administrative Code section 3.827.

min_capital.Captive insurance company: Unencumbered capital and surplus, or the equivalent, in an amount the commissioner determines after considering premium written, the assets held, reinsurance arrangements, the type of business, underwriting practices and procedures, and any other operational criterion the commissioner finds significant. The amount may not be less than $250,000 (Texas Insurance Code section 964.056(a) and (b)).
min_capital.Captive exchange: A captive exchange is formed as an exchange and, except as its subchapter provides, operates as a captive insurance company (section 964.102). No dollar floor different from section 964.056 was stated for an exchange.
min_capital.Form: United States currency; an irrevocable letter of credit in a form the commissioner approves, not secured by a guarantee from an affiliate, naming the commissioner as beneficiary and issued by a bank the commissioner approves; bonds of this state or of a Texas county or municipality; or bonds or other evidences of indebtedness of the United States whose principal and interest are guaranteed by the United States (section 964.056(c)).

tax_notes: Insurance Code section 223A.003 imposes an annual tax of one-half of one percent of a captive insurance company's taxable premium receipts. Taxable receipts include gross premiums, membership fees, assessments, dues, revenues, and other considerations for any kind of insurance written on any kind of property or risk, without regard to where the property or risk is located. They do not include premiums received from another authorized insurer for reinsurance, returned premiums, dividends paid to policyholders, or premiums excluded by another Texas law. There is no deduction for premiums the captive pays for reinsurance. The annual minimum aggregate tax is $7,500 and the annual maximum aggregate tax is $200,000. The tax is due not later than 1 March. A captive whose net tax liability for the previous calendar year exceeded $1,000 makes semiannual prepayments on 1 March and 1 August. A credit is allowed for examination and evaluation fees paid to the state during the year, within the limits in section 803.007. Gross premiums taxed under Chapter 223A are not subject to other taxes, surcharges, or regulatory assessments or fees under the Insurance Code except insurance maintenance taxes under section 964.068. That maintenance tax applies to correctly reported gross premiums from insurance on risks located in Texas, at the line-of-business rates the commissioner sets. The Comptroller states the same 0.5 percent rate, $7,500 minimum, and $200,000 maximum. A single captive maintenance-tax percentage was not published.

types_allowed: Captive insurance companies insuring the operational risks of affiliates and the risks of a controlled unaffiliated business
Captive exchanges, which are reciprocal or interinsurance exchanges

fees.licensing_incorporation: Application fee of $1,500, or a greater amount the commissioner sets by rule to recover the cost of administering section 964.057 (Texas Insurance Code section 964.057(c)). TDI's captive page uses the certificate of authority application FIN180 and the company licensing fee transmittal FIN321. No greater fee was found in the materials reviewed. Secretary of State formation fees are separate and are not set in Chapter 964.
fees.annual_fees: No separate annual captive certificate-of-authority renewal fee is stated in Chapter 964. The annual charges are the Chapter 223A premium tax and the section 964.068 maintenance tax on Texas risks.
fees.premium_tax_rate: 0.5 percent of taxable premium receipts. Annual minimum $7,500 and annual maximum $200,000. Due 1 March, with semiannual prepayments on 1 March and 1 August when the prior year's net tax liability exceeded $1,000. Reinsurance premiums received from another authorized insurer are excluded, and premiums paid for reinsurance are not deductible. Maintenance tax under section 964.068 is additional and is set by line of business.

annual_filing_requirements: On or before 1 March, a captive files a statement of financial condition verified by two executive officers, in the format the commissioner prescribes. On or before 1 June, it files a year-end report of its financial condition with an independent certified public accountant's opinion (Texas Insurance Code section 964.060). The commissioner may allow a fiscal year-end: the annual report is then due not later than the 60th day after fiscal year-end, the audited report not later than the 150th day after the annual report is due, and a balance sheet, income statement, and statement of cash flows verified by two executive officers is still filed before 1 March to support the premium-tax return. The commissioner may waive the actuarial report if net written premium or reinsurance assumed is less than $1 million, or if the company had been in operation for less than six months at the end of the previous calendar year. TDI's captive filing instructions also require the annual statement in Excel, an actuarial opinion or waiver affidavit, and financial projections every third year, and they point captive insurers that are part of a holding-company system to Insurance Code Chapter 823. The Chapter 223A premium-tax report is due on the 1 March tax due date. The governing body holds at least one meeting each year in Texas (section 964.055).

name: The Bahamas
summary: The Bahamas licenses captives as restricted external insurers under the External Insurance Act, 2009 (Chapter 348), supervised by the Insurance Commission of The Bahamas. A restricted external insurer may cover its members, subsidiaries and affiliates, reinsureds who acknowledge in writing that it is restricted, and other persons the Commission approves. Unrestricted external insurers may write broader business from The Bahamas. Cell programmes use segregated accounts companies under the Segregated Accounts Companies Act (Chapter 369C). The Commission does not publish a current captive or external-insurer census; the statistics page covers domestic general and long-term business, and the latest files there run through 2022. Capital for a restricted insurer is the amount the Commission approves. The prescribed floors for unrestricted insurers are B$100,000 for general business, B$200,000 for long-term business and B$300,000 for both. The annual licence fee is B$2,500 for a restricted insurer and B$3,500 for an unrestricted insurer. Section 52 of the Act gives a licensed external insurer a 20-year exemption, running from the date of its first licence, from Bahamian taxes, fees, duties and imposts other than provisions of that kind already in force when the Act commenced and other than licence charges under the Act. Audited financial statements are due within four months of the financial year-end. The Commission has posted a Draft External Insurance Act, 2025; this profile follows the 2009 Act and the 2010 regulations.

The Insurance Commission also publishes a Draft External Insurance Act, 2025, which is not treated as in force here.

tax_notes: The External Insurance Act does not impose a premium tax. Section 52 exempts a licensed external insurer, for 20 years from the date of its first licence, from any tax, fee, duty or impost in The Bahamas, other than provisions of that kind in force when the Act commenced and other than amounts payable for a licence under the Act. The standing annual charge is the licence fee.

fees.licensing_incorporation: B$250 application for an external insurer licence; B$250 application for a segregated account of an external insurer; B$100 application for an insurance manager or external insurance broker. fees.annual_fees: Restricted external insurer B$2,500; unrestricted external insurer B$3,500; insurance manager B$1,000; external insurance broker B$1,000. Late payment adds 10, 15, 20 or 25 percent of the amount due, according to the quarterly ageing of the overdue fee.
fees.premium_tax_rate: No premium tax under the External Insurance Act. Section 52 provides a 20-year exemption from other Bahamian taxes, fees, duties and imposts, subject to the carve-outs in that section. The annual regulatory charge is the licence fee above.

annual_filing_requirements: Audited financial statements, complying with international accounting standards or another standard the Commission determines, are due within four months after the financial year-end, or any longer period the Commission allows. They must be audited by a Commission-approved auditor and accompanied by the auditor's report and by the auditor's certificate on the statutory books, compliance with the section 31 solvency test at the balance-sheet date, and compliance with anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorist-financing reporting. The Commission may also require an actuary's certificate that reserves are adequate. A licensee whose outstanding claims, including incurred-but-not-reported claims, exceed 200 percent of capital and surplus must file an annual actuarial review of those claims. A licensee incorporated outside The Bahamas must, within four months of year-end, file a certificate from its overseas regulator. Each licensee must maintain a resident representative in The Bahamas. The external-insurer licence is renewable annually.

name: Utah
summary: Utah licenses captives under the Utah Captive Insurance Companies Act, Title 31A, Chapter 37, administered by the Utah Insurance Department Captive Insurance Division. The chapter covers agency, association, branch, industrial insured, pooling, pure, risk retention group, sponsored, special purpose, and special purpose financial captives, and cells of a sponsored captive may be protected cells or incorporated cells. The Division's year-end 2025 workbook, provided by Director Travis Wegkamp on 5 November 2026, counts captives and cells together as risk-bearing entities (RBEs). Year-end 2025 was 605 RBEs: 352 pure captives, 3 group captives, 20 cell structures, 222 series/cell captives, and 8 other (pools and agencies). In 2025 the workbook records 172 formations (41 pure, 5 cell structures, and 126 series/cell) and 31 captive licences surrendered (27 pure, 1 cell structure, and 3 series/cell). It shows a dash, not a number, for 2025 formations and surrenders in the group and other columns; those year-end counts are 3 group captives and 8 other in both 2024 and 2025. Year-end 2024 was 464 RBEs: 338 pure, 3 group, 16 cell structures, 99 series/cell, and 8 other. Year-end captive premium was USD $4,130,262,068 in 2024 and USD $3,500,139,380 in 2025. The Division states that the decrease is accounted for entirely by 1 captive, a large commercial carrier no longer using its captive as a reinsurance pass-through, which accounts for a $1B decrease in gross premium. Year-end captive assets under management were USD $13,138,451,175 in 2024 and USD $14,531,806,939 in 2025. A certificate of authority expires annually and is renewed by 1 July. The governing body meets at least once a year in Utah, with a quorum and at least one out-of-state individual physically present, unless the captive is a member of the Utah Captive Insurance Association at the highest membership level. The Division's benefits page states that a flat annual fee is charged in lieu of state premium tax. Real and personal property in Utah remains taxable.
legislation: Utah Captive Insurance Companies Act, Title 31A, Chapter 37, Utah Code
applicable_legislation: Title 31A, Chapter 37, Utah Code, including section 31A-37-102 (definitions), section 31A-37-201 (certificate of authority, in-state meeting or Utah Captive Insurance Association membership, and renewal by 1 July), and section 31A-37-204 (paid-in capital). Special purpose financial captive minimum capital is section 31A-37a-302 of the Special Purpose Financial Captive Insurance Company Act, Title 31A, Chapter 37a, enacted in 2008 and still the current published text. The Division also cites section 31A-37-501 and rule R590-238 for the annual statement, economic-benefit statement, audit, and actuarial opinion. The Chapter 37 text used here is the version effective 6 May 2026.

min_capital.Pure captive: USD $250,000 default minimum of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus (Utah Code section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(i)(A)). A reduced option, the greater of 20 percent of total aggregate risk and USD $50,000, exists for a pure captive that is not a pool (section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(i)(B)). The Captive Insurance Division states that this reduced option has never been used.
min_capital.Pure captive acting as a pool: Not less than USD $250,000 (section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(i)(A)). The reduced option in section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(i)(B) does not apply to a pure captive acting as a pool.
min_capital.Agency captive: The Captive Insurance Division treats an agency captive as a subgroup of a pure captive. The minimum is the pure-captive default of USD $250,000. Section 31A-37-204(2) does not state a separate dollar floor for an agency captive.
min_capital.Sponsored captive: Not less than USD $250,000, of which a minimum of USD $50,000 is provided by the sponsor (section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(iv)).
min_capital.Cell: Section 31A-37-204 does not set a cell floor. The Division's basics page states that a cell has no regulatory minimum and that the sponsor sets it.
min_capital.Special purpose captive: An amount determined by the commissioner after considering the business plan, feasibility study, and pro formas, including the nature of the risks to be insured (section 31A-37-204(2)(a)(v)).
min_capital.Special purpose financial captive: Not less than USD $250,000 of unimpaired paid-in capital and surplus on the day the certificate of authority is issued (Utah Code section 31A-37a-302(1), Special Purpose Financial Captive Insurance Company Act, Chapter 37a). Section 31A-37a-302(2) requires the company to maintain not less than USD $250,000 while the certificate is in force.
min_capital.Branch captive: None has been licensed. Section 31A-37-204(2) does not state a separate dollar floor for a branch captive, and no floor is stated here. Section 31A-37-204(4) requires a U.S. trust fund as security for branch liabilities, measured by the capital and surplus required by Chapter 37 plus reserves on business written through the branch, without stating a standalone dollar amount.
min_capital.Form of capital: Required paid-in capital and surplus may be cash or a cash equivalent, an irrevocable letter of credit that the commissioner approves and that is issued by a Utah-chartered bank, a Federal Reserve member bank, or an FDIC member bank, or marketable securities determined under section 31A-37-204(1). The commissioner may require additional capital based on the type, volume, and nature of the business.

tax_notes: The Division's benefits page states that a flat annual fee is charged in lieu of state premium taxes, and that real and personal property owned in Utah is taxed. The basics page states the same: no state taxes, with real and personal property taxes still applying. The annual captive fee published by the Division is USD $7,250 plus a USD $250 e-commerce fee, USD $7,500 in total, and USD $1,000 for a cell. No Utah corporate income tax on captives is stated on those pages.

annual_filing_requirements: The annual statement of financial condition is due before 1 March, verified under oath of two executive officers, and is filed on the Department portal. A statement of economic benefit to Utah is due before 1 March. An audited financial report and a statement of actuarial opinion are due on or before 30 June for the year ended 31 December. A risk retention group also files the applicable NAIC annual statement blank. There is no mandatory examination period. The commissioner may call an examination at any time, and a called examination typically covers the preceding five years, at the captive's cost. The governing body meets in Utah at least annually, unless the captive holds the highest level of Utah Captive Insurance Association membership.

name: Vermont
summary: Vermont is the largest onshore captive domicile in the United States and a premier global captive hub, having pioneered the US industry with the enactment of the Special Insurer Act of 1981 (8 V.S.A. Chapter 141). Regulated by the Vermont Department of Financial Regulation (DFR) Captive Insurance Division—which maintains a dedicated in-house team of analysts and financial examiners—and supported by the Vermont Captive Insurance Association (VCIA), the state had 707 licensed captives ($243.6B in assets and $36.3B in gross written premium) at year-end 2025, with 51 new licences and 27 dissolutions. Vermont licenses nine distinct captive structures, offers a 30-day licensing turnaround, and provides a competitive graduated premium tax capped at $200,000 with a $5,000 tax credit in each of the first two years.
